papers.title: Engineering multi-photon dissipation with a dc-voltage-biased Josephson junction
papers.abstract: Multi-photon dissipation -- a key resource for bosonic qubits -- is usually realized by parametrically pumping a Josephson coupler at the cost of spurious nonlinear terms. Here we instead engineer it using a dc-voltage-biased SQUID, such that these parasitic terms average out. We activate the conversion of one, two, or four photons of a high-Q mode into a single photon of a lossy mode. We characterize the two-photon dissipation by Wigner tomography, establishing dc-biased junctions as a resource for reservoir engineering and a viable route to cat-qubit stabilization.

summary.summary: A dc-voltage-biased SQUID couples a high-Q memory resonator to a lossy buffer mode, engineering single-, two-, and four-photon dissipation through dynamical Coulomb blockade where the energy $2eV$ from Cooper pair tunneling matches multi-photon transitions. The approach suppresses parasitic nonlinearities by construction compared to parametrically pumped couplers, with measured two-photon loss rate $\kappa_2/2\pi = 0.51$ MHz and maximum two-to-one coupling $g_2^{\mathrm{max}}/2\pi = 18.5 \pm 0.5$ MHz.
summary.motivation: Multi-photon dissipation is essential for stabilizing bosonic qubits like cat qubits, but conventional parametric couplers suffer from spurious Kerr and cross-Kerr terms that limit performance at large pump power. dc-voltage-biased junctions offer an alternative where these parasitic terms rotate at the Josephson frequency $\omega_J = 2eV/\hbar$ and average to zero by construction.
summary.method: A SQUID with tunable $E_J/h$ up to 13 GHz was coupled galvanically to memory ($\omega_a/2\pi = 4.04$ GHz, $T_1 = 3.1$ µs) and buffer ($\omega_b/2\pi = 7.56$ GHz, $\kappa_b/2\pi = 85$ MHz) resonators via stepped-impedance filtering; matching $2eV = n\hbar\omega_a - \hbar\omega_b$ activated $n$-to-1 photon swaps, characterized by Wigner tomography using a dispersively coupled transmon ($\chi/2\pi = 1.51$ MHz).
summary.result: Two-photon dissipation was demonstrated with adiabatic-elimination model matching observations at low $E_J$ ($\kappa_2 = 4g_2^2/\kappa_b$), reaching $\kappa_2/2\pi \approx 0.5$ MHz; spurious one-photon loss and dephasing scaled as $E_J^2$, attributed to environmental modes at $\omega_a \pm \omega_J$ and requiring improved impedance filtering to suppress by $\sim 3$ orders of magnitude for viable cat-qubit stabilization.

papers.title: Anomalous Frequency Shift in Low-Loss Superconducting Granular Aluminum Resonators
papers.abstract: Superconducting high-kinetic inductance materials like granular aluminum (grAl) are a versatile part of the circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) toolbox, provided their losses at microwave frequencies are low enough. To further advance the use of grAl in quantum devices, it is indispensable to identify the dominant loss mechanisms. The standard approach pairs electromagnetic simulations of resonator geometry with measured temperature and power dependence of resonance frequency and loss rate. Most materials follow the phenomenological theory of two-level systems (TLSs) at low temperatures, resulting in an initial decrease of the resonance frequency with increasing temperature. In our work, we observe an opposite behavior at the lowest temperatures: The resonance frequency initially increases with both temperature and readout power, contradicting the standard TLS model predictions. We are able to explain a part of the data by an alternative mechanism associated with the effect of superconducting quasiparticles in a granular system with spatially-nonuniform gap. Yet, the observed change in the resonance frequency with temperature is not matched by a proportional change in the loss rate. We also observe anomalous positive frequency responses following high-energy events, characterized by several time scales. While anomalous behavior has been reported previously in grAl, the disagreement with standard models is particularly visible in our devices thanks to their exceptionally low loss rates.

summary.summary: Superconducting granular aluminum (grAl) resonators with quality factors up to $1.85 	imes 10^6$ exhibit anomalous positive frequency shifts with increasing temperature and readout power at $T < 200$ mK, contradicting standard Mattis–Bardeen and TLS predictions. The authors explain the temperature dependence via quasiparticles in a Josephson-junction network with spatially nonuniform superconducting gaps ($\delta\Delta_0 \sim h f_0$), but the observed dissipation remains unexplained by two orders of magnitude at low temperatures.
summary.motivation: Understanding loss mechanisms in high-kinetic-inductance superconductors like grAl is essential for advancing their use in quantum circuits. The exceptional low-loss performance of these devices ($f_0/Q_i \sim 3$ kHz at base temperature) makes previously hidden anomalies visible, requiring theoretical clarification.
summary.method: Seven lumped-element grAl resonators ($f_0 = 5.31$–$7.53$ GHz) with quality factors $Q_i \sim 10^6$ were measured across multiple cool-downs using standard cQED techniques. Temperature ($23$–$300$ mK) and readout power dependencies were characterized; high-energy events from cosmic rays were monitored to extract relaxation timescales. The frequency and loss data were fit against Mattis–Bardeen theory, TLS models, and a granular medium model accounting for gap distribution in the grain ensemble.
summary.result: Frequency shifts reach $50$ kHz but are decoupled from dissipation: the measured linewidth is only $3$ kHz despite large reactive components. A quasiparticle model with $\delta\Delta_0/h = 1.4 f_0 \approx 10.5$ GHz and residual quasiparticle density $x_{qp}^{\text{res}} = 2 \times 10^{-5}$ explains the positive frequency shift and its temperature dependence, while high-power Kerr nonlinearity is $K_0/(2\pi) = -0.54$ Hz/photon, matching theoretical predictions of $0.5$–$5$ Hz/photon.

papers.title: Design and Modeling of the Charge Readout of a SiMOS Quantum Dot with a Single Electron Transistor and CryoCMOS
papers.abstract: Single electron spin qubits trapped in SiMOS quantum dots are a promising technology for scaling to thousand- or million-qubit systems due to their compatibility with mature CMOS manufacturing processes. A readout system that combines a single electron transistor with a custom cryogenic CMOS amplification and digitization chain offers key advantages by avoiding the use of bulky RF components or room-temperature interconnects. We present design techniques and simulation results for an optimized qubit-SET cryoCMOS interface, culminating in the design of the QNDR1 ASIC, the first cryogenic readout ASIC designed under the Quandarum project, which targets the development of a many-channel spin qubit based detector for use in high energy physics.

similar_to.title: A digitally controlled silicon quantum processing unit

summary.summary: This paper presents design techniques and compact models for a cryogenic CMOS readout ASIC (QNDR1) that combines a single electron transistor (SET) with integrated amplification for SiMOS quantum dot spin qubits. The work includes the first Verilog-A models for double-island and asymmetric-sensing-dot SETs, a 22 nm FDSOI cryogenic PDK at 3.8 K, and simulation results demonstrating $22.5$ to $106.2$ MV/A gain with input-referred noise of $32$ pA rms and power consumption dominated by preamplifier stages consuming $10$–$16$ µW.
summary.motivation: Scalable readout of silicon spin qubits requires integration of sensitive charge detection with cryogenic amplification to avoid bulky RF components and room-temperature interconnects, necessitating careful co-design of SETs with cryoCMOS circuits.
summary.method: Verilog-A compact models were developed for SISET (using MIB model), DISET, and ASD by fitting to published device data; cryogenic noise was estimated using shot noise with Fano factor $F=1.0$ and $10\times$ scaling of flicker noise from room temperature; QNDR1 integrates two preamplifier variants (charge-sensitive and transimpedance), correlated double sampling, and optional digitization in 22 nm FDSOI.
summary.result: Preamplifier Version B achieved $106.2$ MV/A gain and $13.64$ µW power with $14.55$ V/V SNR; sensing current of $192$ pA ($3\sigma$) with $1$ µs readout time; figure of merit improved substantially versus recent dc-SET ASICs, with simulation across three temperature corners (27°C, −195°C, 3.8 K) and five process corners.

papers.title: Device characterization of Si$/$SiGe double quantum dots using exchange oscillations in Earth's magnetic field
papers.abstract: Exchange-based semiconductor qubits encompass a broad family of encodings constructed from singlet- and triplet-like spin states, several of which are compatible with operation at zero applied magnetic field. Their reliable operation requires characterization of environmental noise, residual idle interactions, and exchange-dependent decay, but this characterization often relies on multi-axis control calibration or deliberately engineered magnetic-field gradients. A simpler zero-applied-field diagnostic is particularly valuable for hybrid semiconductor-superconductor systems, in which magnetic fields can degrade superconducting components. Here, we use the intrinsic magnetic-field gradient produced by residual nuclear spins in isotopically enriched Si/SiGe to implement exchange oscillations between two quantum dots as a characterization tool without a micromagnet, dynamic nuclear polarization, or prior multi-axis calibration. Using Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill exchange sequences, we extend the singlet coherence from $T_2^*=1.17\pm0.02~μ$s to $T_2^{\mathrm{CPMG}}=74.8\pm1.8~μ$s with $N=70$ refocusing pulses. The oscillation phase resolves residual exchange in the tens-of-kilohertz regime and enables it to be mapped across the $(1,1)$ charge cell. These results establish intrinsic-gradient exchange oscillations as a simple, more relevant zero-field diagnostic for exchange-only and related semiconductor qubit encodings that is amenable to rapid, high-throughput device characterization.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates zero-applied-field characterization of Si/SiGe double quantum dots using exchange oscillations driven by residual nuclear-spin gradients, enabling measurement of singlet coherence, residual exchange, and exchange-dependent decay without micromagnets or calibrated multi-axis control. CPMG sequences with up to $N=70$ refocusing pulses extend singlet coherence from $T_2^*=1.17±0.02$ µs to $T_2^{	ext{CPMG}}=74.8±1.8$ µs, while oscillation-phase analysis resolves residual exchange in the tens-of-kilohertz regime across the $(1,1)$ charge cell and reveals a broad decay-rate enhancement between 20–40 MHz exchange frequency.
summary.motivation: Exchange-based semiconductor qubits require characterization of environmental noise, residual idle interactions, and exchange-dependent decay, but conventional methods rely on micromagnets or dynamic nuclear polarization—both problematic for hybrid semiconductor–superconductor systems where magnetic fields degrade superconducting performance. A simpler zero-field diagnostic is therefore valuable for these hybrid architectures.
summary.method: The authors exploit the intrinsic magnetic-field gradient $ΔB_z$ produced by residual $^{29}$Si (800 ppm) and $^{73}$Ge nuclei in isotopically enriched Si/SiGe to drive exchange oscillations in a double quantum dot beneath gates P5 and P6. Exchange pulses act as refocusing elements in a Hahn-echo-like sequence, enabling CPMG dynamical decoupling and sensitive measurement of exchange coupling through oscillation-phase shifts via joint Hamiltonian time-evolution fits.
summary.result: The intrinsic-gradient approach resolves residual exchange of $J_{	ext{res}}/h=30±5$ to $64±8$ kHz across different locations in the $(1,1)$ cell (with $σ_{B_z}/2π=140±6$ kHz extracted from fits), maps its spatial dependence, and identifies exchange-dependent relaxation or leakage producing a broad singlet-decay-rate maximum between approximately 20 and 40 MHz—all without externally applied magnetic field, micromagnet, or prior multi-axis calibration.
